extracted.intended_audience: scholars, graduate students, and researchers interested in philosophy of science, scientific practice, and peer review processes
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative criteria and community preferences used in reviewing research funding applications and publications, and how those criteria function as mechanisms that shape which scientific practices persist. Focuses on what reviewers and scientific communities count as acceptable/important evidence, methods, and problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit with Funding Opportunity Announcement (FOA) aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals must address the specific purpose and scope defined by the FOA (e.g., support studies to evaluate candidate cellular therapies to treat radiation-induced injuries in appropriate in vivo models when administered 24 hours or more post-irradiation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The research should be aimed toward the eventual approval pathway specified by the FOA (example given: U.S. FDA Animal Rule licensure pathway). Availability of targeted funds is intended to increase the frequency of projects addressing that precise problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Builds on existing work in the field
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposal should build on existing work in a given field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is cited as general advice in guidelines for deciding whether a research proposal should receive funding; building on prior work signals relevance and continuity with the community's ongoing research program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow, well-defined problem focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals or funded projects are often expected to tackle specific, narrowly defined problems that the community regards as tractable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding announcements and community preferences often encourage research on narrow problems (the text notes FOAs calling for research on very narrow problems); concentrating on such problems can increase a proposal's likelihood of support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance / significance to the community
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers assess whether the research is important enough to warrant the community's attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In publication review, members of the scientific community exercise expert judgment about whether the research is important enough to deserve attention; importance is a factor in whether a practice will gain entry into the pool of practices available for fruitful interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency and trustworthiness of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the evidence reported is sufficient to warrant the community's trust and acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication reviewers evaluate the sufficiency of evidence; insufficient evidence can prevent acceptance regardless of novelty. This criterion serves as the community's 'last chance' to prevent unsuitable practices from spreading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation (as a review criterion) — exercise caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovation is explicitly one of the review criteria, but reviewers are cautioned about seeming too innovative because paradigm-challenging work may be judged as threatening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NIH quote: 'be cautious about seeming too innovative. Not only is innovation just one of five review criteria, but a paradigm shift can be as dangerous as an earthquake! A reviewer may take a challenge to the status quo as a challenge to his or her world view.' Use measured presentation of novelty given community conservatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical / quantitative accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: A community-level preference for preserving or improving quantitative/numerical accuracy in theories and results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn and the author note that comparison of numerical predictions has successfully closed controversies; communities often demand that new theories at least maintain current degrees of numerical accuracy, and sometimes will actively resist theories that reduce numerical success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to community norms and inclusion criteria (paradigmatic fit)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be considered part of the scientific community (and thus eligible for 'fruitful interaction'), one must satisfy the community's normative commitments—criteria for legitimate problems and acceptable methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paradigms 'define the legitimate problems and methods' of a field; failing to subscribe to them can lead to exclusion from opportunities, even without any communication barrier. Normative commitments determine which problems are admitted as scientific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological reliability / accepted methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation includes whether the methods used are regarded as reliable by the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community preferences about which methods are reliable affect both funding and publication decisions; method reliability is invoked when deciding if evidence and results should be trusted and propagated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility and theoretical fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers consider how plausible a given theory is within the community's standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plausibility is part of the community's assessment criteria alongside importance and method; conceptual fit with prevailing frameworks can affect reception but is not the only mechanism of exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation or policing of practice variants via pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational practices (undergraduate and graduate training) that confine students to established problem-solving strategies function as a criterion for which practices are transmitted and accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogy operates as a mechanism to suppress novelty and preserve favorable theoretical and methodological developments across generations; the degree to which practices are taught affects their reproductive success in the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding-driven prioritization (availability of targeted funds shapes research frequency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of funds devoted to specific problems or approaches increases the frequency of research projects aimed at those problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that deliberate allocation of funding (e.g., massive government support) can rapidly produce research outcomes in the intended direction; thus reviewers and program officers use funding priorities as a lever to shape the space of acceptable proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community assent as the ultimate standard
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'no standard higher than the assent of the relevant community'—community acceptance is decisive for whether a practice is sustained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The community decides which preferences and criteria are active; their collective attitude determines whether measures like predictive success or numerical accuracy will be used as decisive criteria for acceptance and propagation of practices.
